speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE BY SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. A statement made in this house by a minister of the crown with regard to a debate which took place recently, has been contradicted by the premier of a province and raises a question of privilege affecting all members of the house.
Addressing the house on April 26, 1960, the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) made the following statement, as reported on page 3 of the appendix to Hansard of that date:
A few days before his death, Mr. Duplessis stated that he would be in a position to submit, in October, a positive proposition to the ministers from Ottawa. It was the Hon. Paul Sauve who submitted that positive proposition. Federal ministers discussed it with Mr. Sauve and, at the time of his tragic death, only a few details remained to be worked out, which was done during a private interview between Mr. Antonio Barrette, Mr. Sauve's successor, and the Minister of Finance, sponsor of the bill which is now before us.
We have kept our word admirably, because Premier Barrette himself believes that this bill is consistent with the terms of Mr. Duplessis' proposal, which was submitted by Mr. Sauve, and later by Mr. Barrette himself.
According to a report in this morning's Le Devoir, the premier of Quebec, in a statement made yesterday in Joliette, spoke differently:
There was never any question of an agreement with Ottawa, but a decision taken by an autonomous government to settle a thorny problem. Thus, by proudly expressing our will, we finally succeeded in recovering for Quebec $10 million in taxes every year, and the $25 million lying dormant in Ottawa coffers.
We even got the federal government to admit that it will entirely vacate the field of education, thus finally winning out after years of struggle.
Under the circumstances, I think the Solicitor General owes it to himself to explain this contradiction between his own statement in the house and that which was made yesterday in Joliette by the premier of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it might be helpful if I were to make a brief report to the house concerning my visit to Istanbul. As hon. members are probably aware there were two meetings held there, one a week ago yesterday.
The first was a meeting of the foreign ministers representing the five western countries which are members of the ten-nation disarmament committee. The purpose of this first meeting was to prepare advice for the three western heads of government who are to participate in the summit meetings commencing on May 16 in so far as the question of disarmament is concerned; also to consider what progress had been made in the disarmament committee itself and what suggestions should be made to the negotiators acting- on behalf of the five western powers, and finally to prepare a report on disarmament to the NATO council which was to meet during the succeeding three days.
We took General Burns with us to Istanbul because, of course, our main interest there was the question of disarmament, and as you know he is heading the Canadian delegation on this important work. The progress that has been made to date by the disarmament committee has not been very satisfactory. The Canadian government is anxious

Istanbul Meetings on Disarmament that there should be a great deal more done when the committee resumes its sittings early next month.
At this first meeting I urged upon the other four western foreign ministers that everything possible must be done to get these negotiations moving; that it was very important to demonstrate to the five eastern nations on this ten-member committee and also to all other nations of the world that the west is very serious in its attempt to bring about a disarmament agreement.
We made several suggestions which perhaps would be of interest to the house. One was that the summit meeting should give direction to the ten-member committee, that instead of discussing further the general issues they should commence to discuss specific measures of disarmament. Mind you, that would mean that these directions would come from President Eisenhower, Prime Minister Macmillan, President de Gaulle and Premier Khrushchev. We had in mind that a joint declaration or recommendation, whatever you wish to call it, should be made to the disarmament negotiators.
Also we suggested that an attempt might very well be made to work out package deals; that is, take one measure of disarmament in which the west was interested and one of equivalent importance in which the east was interested and try to make a package deal with regard to these two particular aspects of disarmament. For example, the west might offer to negotiate a controlled limitation on force levels and related conventional armaments if the Soviet side would agree to negotiate on the nuclear disarmament measures in stages one and two of the western plan.
We believe this is a practical way to get things moving, and if package deals of that kind could be made in several instances the first thing we would know there would be a worth-while disarmament agreement.
Then we also suggested that when the disarmament committee meets again there should be certain informal off the record meetings of the negotiators. To date they have been having formal meetings, records are kept, and then after a matter of a few weeks the whole record is published, which means, as I am sure all parliamentarians will understand, that there is a great deal of talking for the record. We think it would be very useful if the negotiators could get into a huddle from time to time and really try to work out something among themselves. We do not say there should be no more formal meetings, but we think a mixture of


formal and informal meetings would be very beneficial. We hope there will be recommendations of this kind made by the summit to the 10-member committee.
Our suggestions were received very well by the other western foreign ministers and also, when the NATO council met, they were favourably received in the deliberations of that council.
Then a word or two with regard to the NATO council meeting. It was concerned primarily with preparations for the summit. Most of the time was spent in discussing what the three western heads of government should propose at the summit meeting. There had been three working groups set up; one on disarmament, of which of course Canada was a member; another on Germany and Berlin, of which Germany was a member in addition to the United Kingdom, the United States and France; and also one on east-west relations, which was composed of representatives of the United Kingdom, the United States and France and also one representative from the NATO council.
The council endorsed the report which the disarmament working group had submitted and affirmed it in the following words:
The alliance shares the aim of general and complete disarmament to he achieved by stages under effective international control, and supports the proposals of the western negotiators at Geneva to this end.
The council also made reference to the importance of tying in the United Nations with the work of this disarmament committee. The council asserted their view that these proposals provided the best means of carrying out the United Nations resolutions of November 20, 1959, and also regretted the unwillingness which the Soviet side had shown to discuss specific practical measures of disarmament.
Canada throughout has been very insistent that the United Nations should be kept in this picture. We regard ourselves as speaking on that committee for the various middle and smaller powers who are members of the United Nations, and as this world body has the final responsibility for disarmament we think it is of the greatest importance that it should be kept right in the picture. The secretary general of the United Nations, Mr. Hammarskjold, spoke to the disarmament committee at the last meeting they held, I believe, before recessing at the end of April.
On the question of Germany and Berlin there was a general endorsation of the approach which the three plan to use at the summit, and general agreement that it should be left to the discretion of the three how

best to present the western position in the light of developments at the summit. The NATO council reaffirmed publicly its view that the solution of the problem of Germany can only be found in reunification on the basis of self-determination, recalled its declaration of December 16, 1958, and once again expressed its determination to protect the freedom of the people of West Berlin.
The third broad group of subjects dealt with was east-west relations. This, of course, covers quite a wide area, including exchanges of contacts in cultural and information fields and the possibility of discussing trade, aid and other economic questions with the Soviet at the summit. There was also discussion of the concept of detente, which has become such a popular word-meaning a relaxation of tension, I think-and also the question of peaceful co-existence. The conclusions reached included these, that the NATO members desire a true international detente, by which they mean peaceful co-operation among all states, not merely an absence of hostilities. Then they added a condition. A condition of detente is that it must be applicable to all areas of the world, that peaceful co-existence is unsatisfactory if under its cover the Soviet union continues to engage in propaganda attacks on individual members. There would appear to be a detente in so far as Canada is concerned and the United Kingdom, the United States, France and so on, but evidently the situation is a little different in the case of West Germany and Greece, for example. They are being subjected to propaganda and pressures of various kinds, and the council did decide that a detente should be indivisible; in other words, it should apply to all the nations.
Canada supported the idea that the west should go to the summit prepared to discuss in general terms with the Soviet union problems of trade. We also expressed in the NATO council an interest in having a general discussion at the summit on the problem of limiting the traffic in arms through international reporting arrangements which would apply to both the importing and the exporting countries. In other words, a country which is exporting arms would list the exports with some international agency, and so would the receiving country. This work could perhaps be done by the international disarmament organization which has been proposed by the west, should there be agreement to set up such an organization.
In addition, at the conference there were several very interesting individual statements relating to developments in particular areas, but these are not of a nature which I could properly disclose to the house.
9. 1960
Istanbul Meetings on Disarmament
Just before we left Istanbul and later in London we had word of the incident involving the shooting down of a United States plane. The Canadian government regards this as a very serious incident, and we think it points up very clearly the vital need for a disarmament agreement. If incidents of this kind are to keep occurring, one of these days such an incident might trigger a nuclear war. We think it shows very clearly the need for both sides, the west and the east, to reach an agreement on disarmament.
Mind you, we believe in disarmament under control. An incident like this would not happen if there were a proper inspection system. I remind the hon. members that from time to time the present government has taken the stand that Canada would open her skies to inspection if the Soviet would do the same thing in an equivalent area on the other side of the Arctic. I have, for example-I will not repeat the statements that have been made on this subject by the Prime Minister-a letter the Prime Minister wrote Premier Khrushchev on May 9, 1958 which reads as follows:
If you are really anxious about developments in the Arctic and if you wish to eliminate the possibility of surprise attack across the polar regions, I find it hard to understand why you should cast aside a proposal designed to increase mutual security in that area.
The suggestion had been made earlier by Canada and rejected.
Let me repeat here, Mr. Chairman, that we stand by our offer to make available for international inspection or control any part of our territory, in exchange for a comparable concession on your part. I would hope that you would accept some arrangement along these lines not only as an indication of our good faith but as part of a first, experimental step in building a system of international safeguards against surprise attack. When there is, by your own admission, a danger of nuclear war breaking out by accident or miscalculation, it is difficult for Canadians to comprehend your refusal to engage even in technical discussions intended to explore the feasibility of an international system of control.
I am sure all members of the house will agree with the position of the government, which is that Canada will do everything she possibly can to bring about disarmament under proper controls and with a system of inspection.
I think too that this incident, in addition to showing the need for a disarmament agreement, indicates the importance of the summit meeting which is to be held on May 16. There has been some suggestion in the press that perhaps now there would not be any summit meeting. I submit that it is all the more important now that this has happened that the summit meeting should go ahead. Mind you, it is not going to be any easier because of the increase in tension caused by

I must ask the forgiveness of the house, Mr. Speaker, for trespassing on its time in this way, but finally I should like to make it quite clear that the Canadian government was not aware of these activities, and evidently the United States government was not very much aware of them either. I have here a statement which was issued by the state department of the United States on May 7, and it contains this sentence:
As a result of the inquiry ordered by the President, it has been established that in so far as the authorities in Washington are concerned, there was no authorization for any such flight as described by Mr. Khrushchev.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will join with me in expressing the hope that now that both sides have seen just how serious incidents of this kind can be and just how little it might take to bring a world disaster, the nations of both sides will get down to business and really try to work out an agreement on disarmament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the first one to comment on the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), I am sure I may express to the minister, on behalf of all of us in the house our pleasure at seeing him back in his seat looking fit and vigorous after his arduous assignment.
This is another chapter in a series of undoubtedly important visits for which the minister has made preparations. The one in Turkey is now shortly to be followed by a visit to South America. While the meetings in Istanbul were simultaneous and parallel with the commonwealth prime ministers' conference, one might have thought that before returning to Canada the minister would have gone to that conference and participated in the deliberations during the course of this week. The precedent for such participation at a commonwealth prime ministers' meeting was established at the last two prime ministers' meetings when the former secretary of state for external affairs accompanied the Canadian prime minister.
The minister has said that at the ten power disarmament discussion about which he has given a report not much progress was made in the matter of disarmament, as noted by those at the conference.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may just correct that, I was referring to the meetings of the disarmament committee in Geneva which had taken place earlier.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes; that is why I added the words "as noted by the conference". The minister was obviously less optimistic today in discussing disarmament than he was earlier this session. Then he thought there were very good reasons for thinking that success would result from the ten-power discussions. It may be that the minister now recognizes more and more that disarmament is unfortunately to a very large degree dependent on the solution of major political problems which confront the nations of the world, pre-eminent among those, of course, being the question of Germany. But the minister did say that it was agreed that something must be done, and we note with satisfaction the suggestions made as to what should be done at the summit meetings.
Mr. Speaker, we were already aware that the minister had taken the position at the conference that disarmament discussions might be furthered if there was less emphasis on general concepts than on proposals with regard to specific plans for disarmament. The suggestion of a package deal, of course, is not new, but it is worth trying again. We in this party share the desire and the hope that the minister's tempered optimism this time may be justified.
The minister has reported on the desirability of some informal meetings at the ten-power disarmament talks. That has always been the view of those of us in this party. The minister might have gone further and proposed that Canada take the initiative at the ten-power meetings and suggest bilateral talks on an informal basis, particularly between the United States and the Soviet union, for reasons which I am sure the minister will recognize as obvious, and this without in any way affecting the position or the prestige of the other two great powers.
The minister did not say whether at the NATO meeting, there was adequate discussion of the question of consultation, a matter that has interested this house in regard to defence matters before us this session, and also one that arises out of the very problem which the minister mentioned at the last, involving the shooting down on May 1 of a United States plane some 1,500 miles within the territory of the Soviet union.
The minister said nothing about the announcement yesterday, which undoubtedly must have come to the attention of the

NATO meeting, of the intention of the government of the United States to carry on certain underground nuclear tests.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext: May I point out that this statement was made after the NATO meeting. We did not know about it.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Now the minister answers my observation by saying that this declaration of yesterday by the President had not been brought to the attention of the conference as a whole; but that only points up the importance of more adequate consultation. It is difficult to conceive how the United States can be charged with having satisfactorily discharged her responsibilities in the matter of consultation if that matter was not brought by her to the attention of her NATO partners at the meeting in Istanbul.
We note with satisfaction the observation made the minister-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that the question of nuclear tests is being considered not by the NATO council but by the conference of the three nuclear powers. They are dealing with the question of a nuclear test ban.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
The minister will understand, I am sure, that this elementary fact will be widely appreciated by all members of this house; but it is also closely related to the matter of disarmament. I find it difficult to understand how we can say we are fully consulted about matters having to do directly or indirectly with disarmament if such a fact was not brought to the attention of all the NATO partners.
I was about to say that we concur in the support the minister has given to the observations made by the secretary general of the United Nations, particularly having in mind that his observations had to do with the place of a United Nations police force in the enforcement of a partial or comprehensive system of disarmament.
The minister said nothing about participation by China in a disarmament agreement. This is a matter which has been discussed at the prime ministers' meeting, and it must have been touched upon at the meeting of the NATO council.
The minister did not say anything about whether the United States had given evidence of its desire to give more vigorous support to article II of the North Atlantic treaty. When the question of freer trade and trade on a basis calculated to promote peace was being discussed in the council meeting, one would have expected that Canada would put forward her traditional

Istanbul Meetings on Disarmament view that one of the best ways of making NATO an effective instrument of collective action would be by recognizing the importance of economic as well as political co-operation.
Finally, on the matter of the incident of May 1, the shooting down of a United States plane by the Soviet union, there will be questions by some of us in this party on orders of the day, which we feel would be the most appropriate place to elicit further information. But we all agree with the minister that this is a matter that has engaged the concern and touched the imagination of most people in this country during the past few days. We can only hope that the timing of the incident as well as the incident itself will not in any way prejudice the very important talks which are going to take place within a few days among the four great powers.
I sincerely support the observation of the minister that if the open skies proposal had been accepted by the Soviet union this sort of incident would have become unnecessary. The minister referred to statements by the Prime Minister which relate to the application of the principle of open skies in the Arctic. I would remind the minister of the position taken by his predecessor and the former government in 1955, when they supported a proposal by President Eisenhower that there should be reciprocity of aerial inspection of military establishments both in the United States and the Soviet union. If that proposal had been accepted, international confidence would have been created and incidents of this kind would have been minimized. However, the Soviet union refused to accept the American proposal.
As I mentioned a moment ago, we shall have some questions to ask on the orders of the day. I do want to assure the minister once again that in these matters, despite areas of disagreement and emphasis, there is strong support in this parliament for the objectives which the hon. gentleman has in mind. We feel, however, that with regard to the question of disarmament upon which the hon. gentleman places such importance, and rightly so, there has not yet been produced- and I think the minister will not mind my saying so-either by himself or by the government, any evidence of the kind of constructive intervention that Canada could make in a matter of this great importance. It seems to us that this is not only an occasion when we should have support and unity among like minded nations; it is also an occasion when this country, exercising, as the minister earlier told us, its right of independent

Istanbul Meetings on Disarmament thought and action in the field of foreign affairs, should give more adequate evidence of having done so.

speechtext:
The
members of this group are delighted to see the minister returned in good health and spirits. We had some fears for him, in view of the fact that for many years he had not wandered very far from his own doorstep, and particularly in view of the fact that a number of papers and persons in various parts of Canada have wondered if the minister would suffer from sea sickness, air sickness or home sickness. We see, however, that he travels well, and before pursuing the brief remarks I intend to make I want to compliment the hon. gentleman on the fact that his short European experience is also causing him to become quite a linguist.
I shall comment only very briefly on the minister's most interesting statement. I notice he said the progress to date in the disarmament committee was not very satisfactory, and we note his suggestion recommending that the summit meeting give directions to discuss specific issues. We think there is some validity in that suggestion, and also in the suggestion that there might be a package deal-I think the hon. gentleman later said a practical deal.
We were interested to note the suggestion that off the record discussions might take place. We are of the opinion that results of some usefulness might be obtained from that type of discussion, where people are not talking for the record. Even in this house members are tempted on occasion to speak for the record, for the press though, I might add, very seldom in this corner of the chamber.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON ISTANBUL MEETINGS OF WESTERN FOREIGN MINISTERS AND NATO COUNCIL
speechtext:
I do want to say, with reference to the disarmament committee and the minister's recommendation that the activities of that committee should be related more directly to the United Nations, that we are all in support of that suggestion. In connection with the minister's remarks in general to that effect we simply say that this group supports any honest effort to promote disarmament in the world at this time.
Now I wish to say a word or two about the other matters. As to the German question, I do not intend to deal with that matter on this occasion, because this group holds very strong and definite views with regard to that very important subject which we shall air at the proper time which, I judge, will be when the estimates of the minister's department come before us.


With respect to what the minister termed the incident over the Soviet union, I think that was something of an understatement; I would have said "the tragic incident over the Soviet union" in these particular circumstances. The members of this group have no hesitation in saying that we think this was a stupid action on the part of the military authorities of the United States, and one which indicates a complete lack of a sense of responsibility toward its other partners in the western world. In our opinion it was an irresponsible action which was most unfortunate at this time, and we trust that the minister and the government will protest it in the strongest terms to the government of the United States, and indicate to that government the state of public opinion in Canada on this question at the present time.
I am glad to note that the minister still expresses his hope for results from and strong support for a summit conference.
I would say also, with respect to the announcement that the United States intends to resume underground tests of atomic explosions, that the policy of this party is to work for a discontinuance of nuclear tests of all kinds. The minister has frequently advocated both in this house and in statements before the external affairs committee, a similar policy. We are of the opinion that this great blunder on the part of the United States military authorities should strengthen the determination both of the minister and of the government in the days ahead to pursue unrelentingly a constructive but Canadian foreign policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Has the minister seen reports of the Canada-United States meetings in Boston, in which it was stated that cuts by congress in spending on the Bomarc missile illustrate the need for the United States to remember the impact of its decisions in Canada? Would the minister comment on this conclusion and on the corollary which followed, that there should be more opportunities for frank exchanges of opinion on common problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: BOSTON MEETING OF CANA- DIAN-U.S. PARLIAMENTARY GROUPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for sending me notice of his question. I had read the report appearing in this morning's Montreal Gazette. I would say, as I have said before, that there has been and continues to be close co-operation and consultation both at the administrative and at the military level between Canada and the United States in all matters pertaining to the air defence of this continent. This has involved very close exchanges of opinion on all common problems.
Of course, in so far as the recent recommendations of the House of Representatives and the appropriations committee with regard to the United States defence budget are concerned, no prior information was received by the Canadian government as to what those recommendations would be. All we have received is the printed report issued subsequent to the evidence which was given, the report containing the evidence before the committee. There has been no consultation, and no information has passed between that committee and the Canadian government.

subsubtopic: BOSTON MEETING OF CANA- DIAN-U.S. PARLIAMENTARY GROUPS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: DOGFISH-REQUEST FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF KILLING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. As the hon. member knows, various dogfish killing programs have been tried and none have been entirely satisfactory. The 1959-60 program was not accepted by those engaged in the fishing industry to as great an extent as we had hoped, with the result that only about 40 per cent of the money voted by parliament for that purpose last year has been taken up.
For some time now study has been given to a further modification of this plan to make it more effective. I cannot say at the moment when further action will be taken, until a more practical program is fully evolved.

speakerposition: topic

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext:
May I
direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Has the minister seen the statement made by his parliamentary secretary in a Montreal speech as reported by the Ottawa Journal, in which it is said charges were made that the unemployment insurance fund was being drastically reduced by fraud and "we know fraud exists. To deny its existence would be utter nonsense." Has the minister any comment to make on this statement, and will a thorough and complete investigation of this charge of fraud be instituted at once?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: There have been continuous instances of fraud in unemployment insurance as it pertains to claims for benefits, practically throughout the existence of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Charges of fraud have been laid and, of course, there is quite an effort made to recoup the moneys that have been overpaid. I imagine that charges of fraud will continue to be laid. We keep a watchful eye to see that we catch those who fraudulently accept unemployment insurance benefits.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: Has the minister any doubt about the validity of the figures of live claims for unemployment insurance benefits as given here in the house from time to time? In view of the statement made in the speech in Montreal, has the minister any doubt about the figures?

maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: No relation whatsoever.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: I do not understand the question. Is it whether it is a correct figure that I am giving to the house from time to time. Is that what the hon. member means?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: Perhaps, in order to make the question more clear, I should preface it with what was said, as reported again in the Ottawa Journal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member probably goes too far in quoting. His question is perfectly intelligible. If he would repeat it perhaps the minister would understand it. I think he did not hear it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: The purpose of the question was to ask the minister whether he had any doubt about the validity of those figures which he himself gives from time to time-I think it is at the end of each month-in answer to questions put by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the figures I give in response to questions asked are those supplied to me by the unemployment insurance commission.

maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext:
May I ask
the minister a supplementary question. It has to do with his statement in relation to fraud with regard to unemployment insurance benefits. Will the minister say to what extent fraud has existed, since this appears to leave some cloud over some people receiving unemployment insurance? speakerposition: Minister of Labour

speechtext: Your parliamentary secretary said so.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION OF FUND THROUGH FRAUD
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. It is one of the things that does have some bearing, and it has been going on and will continue to go on. Therefore if we catch it we shall try to recoup the moneys overpaid.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, May 5 the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) asked the Minister of National Revenue whether the C.B.C. proposed to send planes to bring pictures of H. R. H. Princess Margaret's wedding back to Canada, and how much it would cost.

speechtext: I am not sure that the hon. member's question is one that comes under the purview of the Department of Justice. If he wants to ask whether an investigation is being made he may do so, but to ask the minister for an expression of opinion in the way he has seems to be quite out of order.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INVESTIGATION INTO PROPOSED BANK MERGER

No,
Mr. Speaker, there is not. In any event bank mergers, if any should come about, do not come within the anti-combines legislation. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. Donald M. Fleming (for the Prime
Minister) moved:

There are some who treat rules and regard for rules with a measure of impatience, but I think all hon. members will realize how vital are the rules of the house.
The aim of the rules must be to govern our procedures and methods in the house and to assure the orderly, efficient, fair and expeditious dispatch of the public business. Therefore there is a need, from time to time, to examine the rules and determine whether they are best serving these purposes. The business of the house does undergo change, and sometimes these changes in the business

The house, over the years, has been faced with an increasing variety and scope in the business that comes before it to be transacted. There is the problem also of the lengthening of the sessions. Those hon. members who sat in this house in the long sessions of 1955 and 1956, and who attended the double sessions we had in some of the earlier years, will not need to be reminded of the way in which the business of the house has been lengthening the average session. I think all hon. members are aware also, Mr. Speaker, of the fact that the world's judgment of parliamentary institutions in the commonwealth and in the western world can no longer be taken for granted as a favourable verdict. We are judged, in all the parliaments of the commonwealth and the west, by the way we transact the public business as well as by the decisions which are reached and the courses of action upon which we decide.
Five years have passed, Mr. Speaker, since the last revision of the rules of the house was carried out. Prior to that the last previous one was in 1927, and it was not as extensive as the revision of 1955. Actually the committee which tendered its final report in 1955 had sat through six sessions of parliament. This committee study arose, in the first instance, as the result of an amendment introduced by the opposition on June 12, 1951 to a government motion resolving that the house go into committee of supply. It was one of those very rare occasions in this house upon which the government has accepted an opposition amendment to a government supply motion.
The committee was appointed on June 15, 1951. The proceedings and the terms of reference may be found in Votes and Proceedings of that year at page 505. The motion was introduced by the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, and it is probably an interesting reflection on the rate of political mortality in this house that of that original committee appointed on June 15, 1951, my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) and I are the only surviving members in this house. Later the personnel of the committee was enlarged, and in 1955 when it brought in its final report among the members who then constituted the committee and who are still members here are the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) and four members on this side of the house who are now ministers.
There had been earlier reports from the committee and decisions taken in the light of its recommendations to alter the rules of

As the result of one of those recommendations the hours of sitting were changed, the hour of sitting in the afternoon being advanced from 3 p.m. to 2.30 p.m. and the hour of daily adjournment being advanced from 11 p.m. to 10 p.m. As the result of a later decision, the Friday evening session was eliminated and a Friday morning session introduced.
The terms of reference of the committee now proposed under this motion are precisely the same as those under which the earlier committee to which I have referred operated and introduced its final report in 1955. Indeed, from the beginning, in 1951, the committee's attention was directed by the house in these words, "to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business". The interpretation given to those words in the committee year after year, I may say, was broad enough to include improvements that might be judged desirable by other standards as well. The final report of the committee was introduced in June, 1955, and that report may be found at page 705 of Votes and Proceedings for June 14, 1955. It was a very extensive report, occupying some 66 pages of Votes and Proceedings.
The report of the committee was unanimous, although it was quite clear that unanimity was reached only as the result of compromise and some of the members of the committee, myself included, indicated that some elements of the report could only be supported by reason of accepting the report as a whole, on balance. The debate on that report began on July 1, 1955, and the report was finally concurred in on July 12, 1955.
Out of that extensive revision of the rules came some major changes. One calls to mind some of them, Mr. Speaker. First, there was the introduction of the limit on the debate on the speech from the throne, limiting that debate to 10 days in all with morning sessions. The second was the limitation of the debate on the budget to eight days; the third was the limitation of the number of supply motions to six, with a total of 12 days devoted to them; another was a reduction from 40 minutes to 30 minutes in the time accorded any hon. member when speaking in committee. A new procedure was also introduced in respect of the tabling of documents in the house.
Let me say just briefly, Mr. Speaker, that while in every case it might have appeared to some hon. members that the changes had the effect of introducing a curtailment, in some degree or other, of the rights of hon. members to engage in discussion or in otherwise unlimited discussion, I doubt very much

if any hon. members today, after the experience we have had in working under these rules for the last five years, would ever wish to go back to the old rules or to repeal any of those changes that were introduced in 1955.
I am sure hon. members are aware that the mere revision of the rules of the house will not bring to perfection the proceedings of this house. There is the old and continuing problem of the enforcement of the rules. A former clerk of this house, Dr. Beauchesne, once said that if the rules of the house were enforced there would be no need whatever for revision at any time. He was referring particularly to the reading of speeches in the house which, of course, is prohibited by a rule which has been very difficult to enforce. Another of the rules is the one forbidding repetition in debate. There are other factors that must enter into the discharge of public business, such as the observance of the rules; the number of political parties represented in the house; the extent of the co-operation that exists in the transaction of the business, and so on. In addition there are such matters as the use of the committees of the house to transact as much of the business as can usefully and properly be transacted in committees without occupying the time of all hon. members. I think it may be said that committees of the house are being used today to the greatest extent in the history of this house. This leads to a more thorough review of the business of the house referred to such committees. There are some hon. members who will not be so certain that the time of the house has been thereby economized. Similarly, by giving more advance notice of the business of the house a contribution has been made toward expediting that business.
One other matter that was mentioned in earlier debates was the contribution to the expedition of the business of the house that ensues from carrying on debates so far as possible on a continuous, uninterrupted basis.
In connection with this proposed new study of the rules by a committee of the house, suggestions have been made from time to time as to various improvements which might be made in the house. The suggestions, indeed, are numerous and varied. It will be for the committee to study and assess them as it may see fit. There is, of course, Mr. Speaker, the matter of the rule respecting closure. I trust that the committee will be prepared to examine and report to the house on that rule.
Suggestions have been made from time to time about the method by which we vote in the house. One hon. member suggested in an entitled to comment on it, has confirmed in

to the introduction of mechanical devices such as have been employed in the House of the People in India.
Suggestions have been made that there are more supply motions provided for than are necessary. Some quarrel has been taken with the fact that on three of the Mondays precedence is given to private bills over private members' resolutions. Suggestions have been made from time to time about arriving at limited debates by agreement.
These are but a few of the suggestions which have been made from time to time and which I am sure the committee will think it profitable to study and report upon.
May I offer the view that the committee, if the house sees fit to set it up, may well study the means of improving the efficiency of our methods in the house and the dispatch of the public business in the most expeditious manner possible without the sacrifice of the essential rights of members. In this task I think the new committee may enjoy an advantage that was not enjoyed by the committee which sat from 1951 to 1955. At that time all of the members on the government side had had no experience in opposition, and all of the members on the opposition side had had, I think, no experience in government. That situation has been changed since and I think that those or some of those on the committee who are appointed from the government side of the house will have had experience on both sides of the house; and it may be expected now that those, or at least some of those who are appointed from the opposition side will have had experience on both sides of the house. This may well influence the views of members of this committee on some of the questions which come before it.
The committee will have the advantage of having as its-I do not say chairman, but as its, shall I say, moderator-the Speaker of the house. This is a committee that is appointed to assist Mr. Speaker in this study, and the benefit of his experience and his observations will be available to the committee as well as his opinion as moderator of meetings.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members will welcome the action being taken by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Fleming) in moving to set up this committee for the purpose of considering with Mr. Speaker the procedure of the house for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business.
I was happy to note that in his remarks the Acting Prime Minister made it clear that he viewed those words as having the same meaning which was given to them by a previous committee of a previous parliament dealing with this subject. I take it that by his remarks he means he views the work of the committee as that of suggesting improvements in the procedures in the House of Commons. With that we all concur.
I also noticed with interest his reference in the earlier part of his remarks to the world's judgment of parliamentary systems. Any experience I have had in parliamentary matters over the years, and I think I am entitled to comment on it, has confirmed in
3688	HOUSE OF
Appointment of Committee on House Rules me the very strong conviction that of the competing systems of government throughout the world the one system that oilers to all human beings in any given country the best guarantee of the protection of their individual human rights and liberties, and the best method of guaranteeing those rights and liberties and evolving them into a working system regulating their day to day lives in political matters, is the parliamentary system. We are fortunate enough to have inherited that system.
Bearihg in mind the tremendous increase, of necessity, in governmental activities-that is, governmental activities in all manner and types of relationships to the individual citizen of the country-it is well that we examine periodically our procedure to make sure that the machinery through which the elected representatives of the citizens operate is working efficiently and that it gives full opportunity to those elected representatives to well conduct the country's business.
I take it that this is not a party matter; at least, I so view it. I view it as something pertaining to the rights of all members of the blouse of Commons; that is, all members regardless of where their responsibilities may lie, whether as members of the government, whether as government supporters, whether as members of the opposition. It seems to me that the whole basis of our system lies in the guarantee that the individual member, no matter what may be his particular responsibility, has his rights assured so that he may make a government answerable for its action -I shall have something to say on that later in my remarks-or that he may voice a grievance or assert his views as to the wisdom or otherwise of a particular policy. It is the guaranteeing of those rights which is important and, having guaranteed those rights, so organizing and so arranging matters as to make efficient use of the time available in any given parliament.
There is one subject upon which I owe it to myself to express a view. I was somewhat surprised to hear the hon. gentleman refer to the subject of closure. Closure became the subject of political debate on the hustings, and I think all members will agree that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a definite commitment on the question of the closure rule, indicating that the government would deal with it. The hon. minister's remarks today gave an impression which I hope he did not quite intend. That commitment, to which I have referred, having been given by the Prime Minister, I hope it is not the intention to place it on the shoulders of a committee charged with advising Mr. Speaker. A stand has been taken on this subject and


I think the minister will understand my suggestion that, after reflection, he might take a somewhat different attitude. I should hate to see the work of the committee impeded by having to deal with this controversial subject, taken from the shoulders of the Prime Minister and the government of the day where the Prime Minister has placed it by his own actions, having made his representation with regard thereto to the people of this country. I think it is very important that the position of Mr. Speaker, be preserved at all times, and that there should be no question about a burden of this kind being placed on his shoulders. Then I hope the former acting prime minister, who also proved his great ability in an acting capacity in another field, will not misunderstand my remarks on this point, but that note will be taken of them.
With regard to improvements in the procedures of the House of Commons, although we note the hon. gentleman's reference to a quotation from a former illustrious clerk of this place to the effect that there was no need to amend the rules, we must bear in mind that members of the House of Commons are human beings and, as such, have human frailties. This being so, it is necessary from time to time to examine the rules in order to see if they should not be amended. As a matter of fact I, for one, am quite content with the fact that members of the House of Commons have human failings. I think that is a fortunate thing, and I should hate to see any other concept of society being asserted in this country.
An interesting question arises when we come to consider the procedures of the House of Commons. There is, of course, that part of our procedure which relates to the government itself, and which is not governed by the rules. Considerable responsibility lies on the government of the day with regard to bringing forward public business in an orderly way so as to permit the fullest discussion and the fullest assessment of the opinion of the house with regard to it. As an example of what I have in mind, it is interesting to note that we are today discussing this motion to set up a committee on the seventy sixth day of the session. On the last occasion when a subject of this kind was under consideration the debate on the motion to set up a committee was brought forward on the seventh day of the sitting of the house.

This raises the whole question of the timing of the bringing forward of public business for decision by the house. This can only in a very limited way be determined by the rules. All hon. members would probably agree that it is not desirable that a government be unduly restricted by the rules as to the time at which matters are brought forward for debate and discussion; on the other hand, it is highly desirable for the efficient functioning of the House of Commons that the government should exercise great wisdom in the timing of bringing forward items of public business. I am never quite sure whether the leader of the house requires other attributes as well as wisdom as a qualification for that office. Sometimes I think he should be possessed of intuition as well as wisdom. However, this is not intended as a criticism of the government of the day as far as the bringing forward of matters for consideration by this house is concerned. I wish, rather, to point out that this most important part of our daily procedure is not governed to any substantial extent by the rules.
Along with our consideration of this question there is another matter that might be mentioned, namely the whole question of a period of time which ought to elapse between the first reading of a government bill and its coming forward for second reading. It seems to me that a reasonable period of time should elapse between first and second readings of a government bill. For some time I have felt that insufficient attention has been paid to this small, but important, detail, and that the time of parliament could be saved, and a better-a more efficient-debate could take place if a proper period of time were to elapse. I believe that in earlier times, in another of the parliaments about which we have heard so much, there was a requirement of a 10-day delay. That protection has been removed, I believe, though I have not had an opportunity to verify the fact in preparing for this debate.
Then there is the whole question of committees. I have been very much concerned with what I consider to be the substantial damage being done to the procedure in the House of Commons because of the inordinately large number of committees now sitting. I doubt if the government itself realizes -because government members are not usually members of committees-the number of committees which are sitting and the frequency of those sittings. I wish to develop this subject today, because I hope the government will look into the matter.

We now have a sharply increased number of committees sitting. I have not attempted to work out a tabulation but it would seem that we have about twice the number currently sitting that ever sat in any parliament since confederation. Although the government leader suggested bringing the business to a conclusion the other day we have not even at this time set up all the committees for which notice has been given on the order paper or indicated in the throne speech.
That brings me to this point. The practice in former days when there were very few committees was to have large committees. We now have some dozen or so standing committees as well as many special committees. I should like to place on the record the number of members on these standing committees. The committee on privileges and elections consists of 29 members; the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraphs, 60 members; the miscellaneous private bills committee, 50 members; the committee on banking and commerce, 50 members; .the public accounts committee, 50 members; the committee on agriculture and colonization, 60 members; the committee on standing orders, 20 members; the committee on marine and fisheries, 35 members; the committee on mines, forests and waters, 35 members; the industrial relations committee, 35 members; the committee on debates, 12 members; the committee on external affairs, 35 members; the joint committee on printing consists of 23 members of the House of Commons and the joint committee on the library of parliament consists of 21 members of the House of Commons. In addition there are a great number of special and select committees having in each case a very large personnel.
This has brought about a gradual change over the years that has been sharply accentuated in the last two or three years. The large number of members on each committee
3690	HOUSE OF
Appointment of Committee on House Rules means that each member of the House of Commons is on a great number of committees. The committees of necessity must meet concurrently. The result is that we have developed the practice over the last decade or so of having what one hon. member aptly described as a group of nomadic members moving from committee to committee, spending a few minutes at each committee sitting or indeed not attending committee sittings at all or not attending the meeting of a particular committee for days on end.
That is not an efficient way of doing committee work. I would hope that examination would be given to the question of the size of committees and the time of setting them up. The time of setting them up is not governed by the rules but is controlled by the government. The number of members, however, would be a matter for changes in the rules. Those changes could be made if my view is shared by other hon. members who may think it desirable although I recognize that some hon. gentlemen may have sharply differing views. I merely seek to indicate the present difficulty which in my opinion, for what it is worth, the committee ought properly to examine.
There is one other significant thing. A great deal of difficulty arises from committees sitting while the house is sitting. That difficulty would disappear if the committees were smaller. Incidentally, I know one ought not to make personal references but the experience I have had in committee work over the years supports the view that smaller committees are much more effective. The problem of attendance and the problem of conflicts with sittings of the house simply disappear if it is a small committee.
I think it is a legitimate comment to say that many supporters of the government find extensive committee work rather desirable because while technically they have as full an opportunity as anyone else to participate in house debates, in practice they do not always have as full an opportunity as they might wish when debates are limited either by the rules, as with the throne and budget speech debates, or on other occasions. It is simply not mechanically possible with large majorities. Indeed, I noticed that this matter was raised in the early sittings of the earlier committee on procedure. At that time it was thought that the government of the day had a large majority but the present government has an even larger majority than when this point was raised.
If an hon. member could be on one or two committees in a parliament instead of five, six or seven as at present he would find


it possible to attend the sittings of the committee and to take up the subject it is studying as his major and special activity. I have the feeling that it would enable fuller participation in the work of parliament on the part of that committee member. It would provide more effective participation and would give the hon. member an opportunity to develop as an expert on that subject because of his accumulated experience on the committee and his extensive study of the subject.
There are other matters of this nature that could be dealt with. One question that has bothered me is the period of the day in the ordinary day's sitting before orders of the day are reached. I refer to that whole period covered by the routine proceedings, the question period. It seems to me there should be examination given to a more effective use of that period. While I supported the change in the rules made in 1955 I now find in the light of experience one of the changes has represented a retrograde step although many of the changes in the rules I supported at that time have proved effective. The retrograde step to which I refer relates to questions. We now have on the question hour three types of questions, starred questions, written questions on the order paper and oral questions.
In 1955 a change was made concerning questions on the order paper. Instead of having them answered in the House of Commons, which was a very short procedure, they are not now further dealt with in the house at all but rather are answered by the appropriate minister filing with an official of the house the written answer. The appropriate official then sends notice to the person asking the question. That may be done at any time of the day. It is most unsatisfactory from the point of view of the person asking the question. In my view it is also highly unsatisfactory from the point of view of the procedure in the House of Commons and the loss of time involved. A consequence of the inefficiency of that procedure, because of what I have said and also because of the fact that the answers to questions are not printed with other similar types of information in the Hansard record but rather are printed at the end of Hansard, is that an hon. member is virtually compelled to decide whether or not he will make his question a starred question or try to frame it as an oral question. The result is a clumsy thing from the point of view of anyone referring to Hansard, a loss of time in the house itself and an unsatisfactory procedure from the point of view of the one asking the question.
I would hope that that matter could be examined. For my own part I should certainly like to see the written questions

answered at the appointed time during the proceedings in the House of Commons simply by the minister indicating the number of the question if he is answering. This is a very short procedure. It would have the virtue of having the questions printed in the appropriate place in Hansard, and all of this would tend to eliminate the great number of starred questions which require an oral answer, sometimes quite lengthy. It would obviate the necessity of them, and it would also obviate the necessity for asking some of the oral questions on the orders of the day.
There are other matters which require attention. Probably there should be some examination of the reason for and an explanation required when an order of this house is not, for one reason or another-[DOT] sometimes a very good reason-presented to the house within a required limit of time. There are some very bad examples of delay. For some of them there are reasonable explanations. In others, it is not so clear; there is no explanation. But, in any event, these are lesser problems which may require to be looked at. It seems to me they require the attention of the committee.
There is a rather interesting thing about this committee. It will have the benefit of the excellent work by the earlier committee on this subject; it will have the advantage referred to by the former acting prime minister of the day, if I may use an apparent contradiction in terms, and there is also the very good report from the select committee on procedure in the United Kingdom, ordered to be printed February 15, 1959. There is all that great fund of material available.
There is one other matter of which we should take some cognizance. When the changes were made in 1955 concerning the matter of the motion to go into supply it was decided that a vote would be required at a point of time on the evening of the second day. After that period and up until ten o'clock there is an opportunity for any member of the House of Commons to express a grievance against the government of the day. I think that that procedure might be looked at because, with the wider activity of government in an ever widening field-and that process has been continuing for many years and I expect it will continue as time goes on-it is desirable that some clear opportunity be given a private member to assert a grievance against the government; also that the appropriate minister concerned be given a designated opportunity to reply. As the procedure now stands, if there is an amendment to the amendment of the motion to go into supply, the amendment to the

It is a small thing, but the extra 15 minutes or 20 minutes there could be very useful and better used in the interests of parliament, in the interests of governing the affairs of the country, by a private member asserting a grievance with correspondingly an appropriate amount of time given to a minister. It may be necessary or desirable, Mr. Speaker, to strengthen this right of members to assert grievances, in view of the changed procedure and the limitation of the time taken for the supply motion, but also in delimiting it to protect the government and the appropriate minister in making a reply. In other words, the former practice, prior to the change in the rules, was that a supply motion was not restricted to any given length of time. All the minister had to do was to wait and then to take as much time as he wished to reply. That was not satisfactory; but there is, however, a period of an hour and 10 minutes or an hour and 15 minutes for the whole matter of grievances. That whole subject should be looked into.
Under the old procedure there was no limit of time for a statement of grievances by members of the House of Commons and there was a tendency in deference, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this was a difficulty that I am sure all Speakers had-to have a general debate on the subject of whatever the grievance was. It is a very difficult point to determine.
There is a whole subject there because this matter of voting supply is one of the most important functions of the House of Commons. We have, I think appropriately, limited the time of the supply motions but we have not sufficiently protected the use of the remaining time for the assertion of grievances or the statement of grievances by individual members of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to prevent the house from hearing the leader of the C.C.F., but if I may be permitted to take a moment I should like to continue.
My view of the whole matter is that it is of the utmost importance, at a time in human society when there are competing systems and when our system, as was correctly stated by the minister in moving the motion, is under the test of world opinion, that we take cognizance of just what our practices and procedures are.
Without wishing to trespass on the time of the house although the rule gives me the right to do so-I will not take more than a very limited time. I want to make reference to an editorial which I read in the Ottawa Journal on May 7, 1960, not on this subject but on a related subject. I thought it was very good. It is entitled, "Bureaucracy Must Be Kept Under Constant Watch". The point of the editorial had to do with a speech delivered by Viscount Kilmuir, Britain's lord chancellor, at the University of Chicago law centre. The editorial contains this quotation from his speech:
Governmental bureaucracy must be kept under constant watch. A large number of regulations affecting the lives and homes of citizens have poured from the government; all manner of tribunals outside the ordinary courts of law have been set up... Procedures have been devised which appear to many of us to be dangerously restrictive of the liberty of the subject.
Then the editorial goes on to say:
Our modern economy being what it is, life now being so desperately complex, governments are compelled to delegate authority, to set up boards and commissions to do things which they themselves cannot do. But this should never be permitted to mean that the citizen is deprived of his rights, and especially of the inalienable right of his day in court.
That is what is meant by the saying about eternal vigilance being the price of liberty. And this vigilance, it should be added, is not something


to be exercised with respect to bureaucrats alone; it must be applied to cabinets as well, to cabinets whether they are Liberal, Conservative or of any party whatsoever.
The editorial was not intended to apply directly to the subject now under discussion, Mr. Speaker, but I think it does. In my opinion it is very relevant and important. The government of necessity is engaged in a great number of activities but the necessity of the government, because of the volume of public business to be brought before the House of Commons, to seek methods to expedite the business of the house should never be permitted to bring about a situation where any member of the House of Commons elected as the representative of citizens of this country is deprived of his rights and especially of his inalienable right to his day of argument on the point at issue.
The observation in the editorial that the price of the preservation of our system, with the benefits which I believe it confers on the human beings making up this country, is eternal vigilance is equally applicable. There must be eternal vigilance over the practices of parliament, over the correct procedures to apply to assure all members that their rights will be preserved, to assure the government of its right to bring forward its business and have it dealt with, to assure individual members of the opposition of their right to bring forward their grievances and to assure them of their right to make the government answerable to the elected representatives of the people.
In welcoming this motion, Mr. Speaker, I express the wish that the work of the committee may be useful in improving and strengthening our system of government.

Mr. Speaker, I said a moment ago that I was quite sure that a committee working with you as moderator would have every possibility of reaching some general agreement on proposed changes in the rules. I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he says that our type of society and our parliamentary system in the western world are on trial today and that it behooves us to do everything we can to make them efficient and, I would add, to make them operate in the interests of the ordinary citizen of this country. The rules of the House of Commons are absolutely essential to our parliamentary system of government. These rules make provision for the government to accept its responsibility as the government of the country and for the government to accept the responsibility of introducing legislation into the House of Commons, but they also give members of parliament, particularly members of the opposition, the right within the rules to speak

out, to commend if desirable and to criticize at length anything that we feel is undesirable.
The basic foundation of our parliamentary procedure is set out in Beauchesne, third edition, citation No. 1. That citation reads as follows:
The principles that lie at the basis of English parliamentary law, as Bourinot so aptly says, are: "to protect a minority and restrain the improvidence or tyranny of a majority; to secure the transaction of public business in an orderly manner; to enable every member to express his opinion within limits necessary to preserve decorum and prevent an unnecessary waste of time; to give abundant opportunity for the consideration of every measure, and to prevent any legislative action being taken upon sudden impulse." In a close contest when the house is considering a highly controversial measure, the positions of parties are equalized; the government side may rely on its majority but the opposition is strengthened by the rules of procedure which both are bound to preserve and which the Speaker must enforce.
I believe that the members of the opposition parties who comprise the minority have the right to criticize legislation at length, at great length if in their opinion they feel it desirable, but that the government and parliament itself have the right to come to decisions on various questions before the house.
As the Minister of Finance has said, a committee of the house made a report in 1955. As a matter of fact, the changes then were really the first and only substantial alteration in the rules of the house since confederation. On other occasions steps have been taken to change the rules but these steps involved particular circumstances and the changes were not widespread.
In 1912 and 1913 a filibuster occurred and there was consideration of rule changes following the filibuster. In 1927 certain reforms were instituted but again not of the widespread nature of the reforms in 1955. After changes were made in the rules of the house in 1927 we went on for a number of years before any further move was made to alter the rules. The next motion to appoint a committee was moved in May, 1940, but further action was not taken because of the special emergency war conditions at that time. In 1944 a procedural committee made certain proposals which were studied in committee of the whole but never reached the house for decision. In 1946 a similar committee was appointed. In 1947 a report was made. On January 25, 1948, the Speaker's report was tabled in the House of Commons but nothing was done to bring it into effect. As the Minister of Finance has said, we continued until 1951 when a further committee was established and as the culmination of its work over a long period of time changes in the rules were adopted in 1955.

I am not one of those who view parliamentary proceedings, as they now are, with great impatience. I am not one of those who feel that one of the most important things is to shorten the session and get out before a certain target date, to wrap up the business so that members can proceed to some other occupation. As I see it, the work of a member of parliament is becoming more and more a fulltime occupation. While we are always open to consider proposed changes in the rules which may be of benefit, those changes should not be hastily arrived at and the objective should not be to have a parliamentary session of a particular number of days or a particular length of time. These are not the main objectives that we should be considering in discussing the procedures of this house. I am all for the expeditious conduct of the business of the House of Commons; I am in favour of that, but one should not assume that it is always the opposition that carries on a given debate for a length of time or that that is the reason a certain procedure is taking a long time.

We had some changes in the rules in 1955, and I think in general the changes in the rules were beneficial. But I do want to point out some of the disadvantages that I feel have resulted from those changes in the rules. We have a fixed throne speech debate of ten days. We have a fixed budget debate of eight days. This may be resulting, I am not sure, in a shorter throne speech debate and a shorter budget debate than would otherwise occur. I think probably it means a shorter throne speech debate because of the morning sittings. But what has been the result? I think there is a tendency when you embed a closure rule in the book or a series of closure rules-and that is what they are- to remove much of the vitality of the House of Commons. Reports go abroad, and I feel they are accurate generally, which say that when we have a fixed debate of one day on something, or two days, or ten days on the throne speech or eight days on the budget, the debates are dead, they are inconsequential, and everyone is just waiting around until the vote is called. The only thing you can draw from that is that we could have either wide open-ended debates or perhaps we could look at the length of the debate provided by the rules themselves. I refer to the periods of time allowed for consideration of private and public bills.
